title: Channels
intro: Channels send values from one thread to another. Sending a value moves it into the channel.

coming_from.go: `mpsc::channel()` is a queue that grows, so `send` does not wait for the receiver the way a send on `make(chan T)` does. `sync_channel(n)` is `make(chan T, n)`, and `sync_channel(0)` is the unbuffered kind. There is no `close`: the channel ends when every sender is dropped, and there is no `select` in the standard library.
coming_from.kotlin: A channel is like a `LinkedBlockingQueue`, but `send` moves the value in, so the sender can't touch it afterwards, and only one thread receives (a Kotlin coroutine `Channel` may have several receivers; a Rust `Receiver` cannot be shared). When every sender is dropped the channel closes and `for msg in rx` ends, so no `"DONE"` marker is needed.
coming_from.python: A channel is like `queue.Queue`, and `for msg in rx` stops by itself when every sender is gone, so you don't need a `None` marker (or `shutdown()`, new in Python 3.13). `send` moves the value, so the sender can't change it afterwards.
coming_from.typescript: A channel is like `postMessage` between workers, except that `postMessage` copies the data (unless you transfer it) and `send` moves it. `for msg in rx` blocks a thread, with no callback, until every sender has been dropped; a `MessagePort` has no such count.
coming_from.java: `mpsc::channel()` is a `LinkedBlockingQueue`, but `send` moves the value, so the sender can't touch it afterwards. The channel closes by itself when every sender is dropped, so no `DONE` marker is needed.
coming_from.csharp: `mpsc::channel()` is `Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>()`, and `for msg in rx` is `await foreach` over `ReadAllAsync()`, except it blocks a thread instead of awaiting. Dropping the last `tx` closes it like `Writer.Complete()`, and `send` moves the value so the sender can't change it later.
coming_from.c: C has no channels, so you'd build a queue with a mutex and a condition variable (or use a pipe for bytes). `mpsc::channel()` is that queue, ready made; it closes when the last sender is dropped, and the compiler stops the sender from using a value after sending it.
coming_from.cpp: The standard library has no channel, so `mpsc::channel()` replaces your mutex, `condition_variable` and queue class. `send` moves like `std::move`, but Rust then rejects any later use of the moved-from variable, which C++ accepts.

notes: `mpsc` means multiple producers, single consumer. Clone `tx` to have several senders; the receiver cannot be cloned.
You never call `close`. The channel closes when every sender has gone away, here when the thread ends, and `for msg in rx` ends with it.
`send` returns a `Result`, because the receiving side might already be gone. `.unwrap()` here means "crash if nobody is listening".

gotcha.title: Changing a value after sending it
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Java, Kotlin, C#, Python and C you can send a list and keep changing it. The receiver holds the same list, so it sees your later change, at a moment you don't control: two threads use one list and nothing orders their accesses.
gotcha.rust_sees: `send(msg)` moves `msg` into the channel. After that line, the sending thread doesn't own it anymore, so it can't touch it.
gotcha.why: Once you send something, it belongs to the receiver. The sender can't touch it anymore, so two threads never fight over it, and the compiler checks this for you.

kotlin.says: Kotlin printed receiver sees [99, 2]. The queue passed the same list object, not a copy, so the sender's change after `put` showed up on the other side.
kotlin.code:
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue
import kotlin.concurrent.thread

fun main() {
    val queue = LinkedBlockingQueue<MutableList<Int>>()
    val receiver = thread {
        val got = queue.take()
        Thread.sleep(10)
        println("receiver sees $got")
    }
    val msg = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    queue.put(msg)
    msg[0] = 99     // sender keeps changing what it already sent
    receiver.join()
}

python.says: Python prints receiver sees [99, 2]. The queue passes the same list object, not a copy, so the sender's change after `put` shows up on the other side.
python.code:
import queue
import threading
import time

q = queue.Queue()


def receive():
    got = q.get()
    time.sleep(0.01)
    print("receiver sees", got)


r = threading.Thread(target=receive)
r.start()

consumers.py.code:
import queue
import threading

# queue.Queue allows several consumers. One None marker stops only one of them.
q: queue.Queue[int | None] = queue.Queue()
stopped = []
still_waiting = []


def consume() -> None:
    try:
        if q.get(timeout=0.3) is None:
            stopped.append(1)
    except queue.Empty:
        still_waiting.append(1)  # nothing more arrived: it would have waited for ever


consumers = [threading.Thread(target=consume) for _ in range(2)]
for t in consumers:
    t.start()
q.put(None)  # one marker for two consumers
for t in consumers:
    t.join()
print("consumers that saw the marker:", len(stopped))
print("consumers still waiting:", len(still_waiting))

# Either side can shut a Queue down: after a consumer calls shutdown(), put raises
q2: queue.Queue[int] = queue.Queue()
q2.shutdown()
try:
    q2.put(1)
except queue.ShutDown:
    print("put after the consumer's shutdown(): queue.ShutDown")

others.py.code:
import asyncio
import multiprocessing as mp
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import time


def child(q) -> None:
    data = q.get()
    data.append(99)  # changes the child's copy only


async def aio() -> None:
    q: asyncio.Queue[int] = asyncio.Queue()
    q.put_nowait(1)
    print("asyncio.Queue.get:", await q.get())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # multiprocessing.Queue pickles what you put: the receiver gets a copy
    q = mp.Queue()
    data = [1, 2]
    q.put(data)
    p = mp.Process(target=child, args=(q,))
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print("multiprocessing.Queue: the sender's list is still", data)

    # ThreadPoolExecutor.map returns results in input order, whichever finishes first
    def slow_first(x: int) -> int:
        time.sleep(0.05 if x == 3 else 0)
        return x * x

    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:
        print("ThreadPoolExecutor.map:", list(pool.map(slow_first, [3, 1, 2])))

    asyncio.run(aio())

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.*

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val ch = Channel<Int>() // RENDEZVOUS, capacity 0
    println("trySend with no receiver: ${ch.trySend(1).isSuccess}")

    val sender = launch {
        println("sender: send(2)")
        ch.send(2)
        println("sender: send(2) returned")
    }
    yield() // let the sender run: it suspends in send
    println("main: still running, sender done = ${sender.isCompleted}")
    println("main: receive = ${ch.receive()}")
    sender.join()
}
